L0@P0: Accepting Optimally in Automated Negotiation with
L1@P0: Incomplete Information
L2@P0: Tim Baarslag
L3@P0: Interactive Intelligence Group
L4@P0: Delft University of Technology
L5@P0: Mekelweg 4, Delft, The Netherlands
L6@P0: T.Baarslag@tudelft.nl
L7@P0: Koen Hindriks
L8@P0: Interactive Intelligence Group
L9@P0: Delft University of Technology
L10@P0: Mekelweg 4, Delft, The Netherlands
L11@P0: K.V.Hindriks@tudelft.nl
L12@P0: ABSTRACT
L13@P0: When a negotiating agent is presented with an offer by its
L14@P0: opponent, it is faced with a decision: it can accept the offer that is currently on the table, or it can reject it and
L15@P0: continue the negotiation. Both options involve an inherent
L16@P0: risk: continuing the negotiation carries the risk of forgoing
L17@P0: a possibly optimal offer, whereas accepting runs the risk of
L18@P0: missing out on an even better future offer. We approach the
L19@P0: decision of whether to accept as a sequential decision problem, by modeling the bids received as a stochastic process.
L20@P0: We argue that this is a natural choice in the context of a
L21@P0: negotiation with incomplete information, where the future
L22@P0: behavior of the opponent is uncertain. We determine the
L23@P0: optimal acceptance policies for particular opponent classes
L24@P0: and we present an approach to estimate the expected range
L25@P0: of offers when the type of opponent is unknown. We apply
L26@P0: our method against a wide range of opponents, and compare
L27@P0: its performance with acceptance mechanisms of state-of-theart negotiation strategies. The experiments show that the
L28@P0: proposed approach is able to find the optimal time to accept, and improves upon widely used existing acceptance
L29@P0: mechanisms.
L30@P0: Categories and Subject Descriptors
L31@P0: I.2.11 [Artificial Intelligence]: Distributed Artificial Intelligence—intelligent agents, multi-agent systems
L32@P0: General Terms
L33@P0: Algorithms, Experimentation, Performance, Theory
L34@P0: Keywords
L35@P0: Negotiation; Acceptance strategy; Optimal stopping
L36@P0: 1. INTRODUCTION
L37@P0: Suppose two parties A and B are conducting a negotiation, and B has just proposed an offer to A. A is now faced
L38@P0: with a decision: she must decide whether to continue, or to
L39@P0: accept the offer that is currently on the table. On the one
L40@P0: hand, accepting the offer and ending the negotiation means
L41@P0: running the risk of missing out on a better deal in the future.
L42@P0: Appears in: Proceedings of the 12th International Conference on Autonomous Agents and Multiagent Systems (AAMAS 2013), Ito, Jonker, Gini, and Shehory (eds.), May,
L43@P0: 6–10, 2013, Saint Paul, Minnesota, USA.
L44@P0: Copyright
L45@P0: c 2013, International Foundation for Autonomous Agents and
L46@P0: Multiagent Systems (www.ifaamas.org). All rights reserved.
L47@P0: On the other hand, carrying on with the negotiation involves
L48@P0: a risk as well, as this gives up the possibility of accepting one
L49@P0: of the previous offers. How then, should A decide whether
L50@P0: to end or to continue the negotiation?
L51@P0: Of course, A’s decision making process will depend on
L52@P0: the current offer, as well as the offers that A can expect
L53@P0: to receive from B in the future. However, in most realistic
L54@P0: cases, agents have only incomplete information about each
L55@P0: other [5, 9, 15]. In this paper, we explore in particular the
L56@P0: setting where the opponent has only limited or no knowledge
L57@P0: of A’s preferences, and the proposals that A receives will
L58@P0: therefore be necessarily uncertain. This makes A’s task of
L59@P0: predicting B’s future offers by no means an easy one.
L60@P0: Moreover, predicting B’s future offers is only part of the
L61@P0: solution: even when A can predict B’s moves reasonably
L62@P0: well, A still has to decide how to put this information to
L63@P0: good use. In other words, even when a probability distribution over the opponent’s actions is known, it is not straightforward to translate this into effective negotiation behavior.
L64@P0: As an extreme example, consider an opponent R (for Random) who will make random offers with utility uniformly
L65@P0: distributed in [0, 1]. Suppose furthermore that we can expect to receive two more bids from R until the deadline
L66@P0: occurs. R currently makes an offer of utility x ∈ [0, 1]; for
L67@P0: what x should we accept? Of course, an even better bid
L68@P0: than x might come up in one of the two remaining rounds;
L69@P0: on the other hand, it might be safer to settle for this bid
L70@P0: if x is large enough. For this particular case, we will prove
L71@P0: that there is an optimal acceptance strategy, and we show
L72@P0: exactly for what x to accept (see Section 3).
L73@P0: The main contribution of this paper is that we address
L74@P0: both of A’s problems: first, at every stage of the negotiation, we provide a technique to estimate the bidding behavior of various opponent classes by modeling A’s dilemma as a
L75@P0: stochastic decision problem. For particular opponent classes
L76@P0: we are able to provide precise models, and to formulate exact mathematical solutions to our problem. For the second
L77@P0: step, using the ranges found earlier, we borrow techniques
L78@P0: from optimal stopping theory to find generic, optimal rules
L79@P0: for when to accept against a variety of opponents in a bilateral negotiation setting with incomplete information. The
L80@P0: solutions proposed are optimal in the sense that there can
L81@P0: be no better strategy in terms of utility.
L82@P0: We begin by introducing our approach in Section 2, and
L83@P0: we apply our methods to find optimal rules in the specific
L84@P0: case of opponents that bid randomly in Section 3. We then
L85@P0-1: build upon these cases and subsequently work out more realistic scenarios in the following sections. In Section 4, weexplore opponents that change their behavior over time, and
L86@P1: we determine optimal stopping rules when good estimates
L87@P1: of their bidding behavior are known. We extend these results by combining our approach with a state-of-the-art prediction mechanism, and we demonstrate that our approach
L88@P1: outperforms existing accepting mechanisms, even when the
L89@P1: opponent’s behavior is unknown.
L90@P1: 2. DECISION MAKING IN NEGOTIATION
L91@P1: UNDER UNCERTAINTY
L92@P1: In this work we focus on a bilateral automated negotiation, wherein two agents try to reach an agreement while
L93@P1: maximizing their own utility. Agents use the widely-employed
L94@P1: alternating-offers protocol for bilateral negotiations [21], in
L95@P1: which the negotiating parties take turns in exchanging offers for a fixed number of rounds N. In case the deadline
L96@P1: is reached before both parties come to an agreement, both
L97@P1: receive zero utility. A negotiation scenario consists of the
L98@P1: negotiation domain, which specifies the setting and all possible bids, together with a privately-known preference profile
L99@P1: for each party. A preference profile is described by a utility function u(x), which maps each possible outcome x in
L100@P1: the negotiation domain to a utility in the range [0, 1]. If an
L101@P1: agent receives an offer x, its acceptance mechanism has to
L102@P1: decide whether u(x) is high enough to be acceptable.
L103@P1: 2.1 Stochastic Behavior in Negotiation
L104@P1: Suppose player B is involved in a bilateral negotiation
L105@P1: with private preference information, and at some point in
L106@P1: time, he has decided that he is satisfied with a utility around
L107@P1: u, called his target utility. However, there are many possible
L108@P1: bids with approximately this utility for player B. As usual,
L109@P1: we call this set of bids X the iso-level bids with utility u.
L110@P1: As player B is indifferent between these bids, B may attempt to optimize player A’s utility in order to maximize
L111@P1: the chance of an agreement. But this is difficult for B to
L112@P1: achieve, as he does not know A’s preferences. When using
L113@P1: the alternating offers protocol, player B cannot simply send
L114@P1: out all considered offers as one bundle, but instead, he can
L115@P1: only offer them sequentially. Player B typically continues to
L116@P1: select different bids from X until his target utility changes;
L117@P1: then a new set of iso-level bids is generated, and the process
L118@P1: starts again. The order in which player B picks bids from
L119@P1: the set of equally preferred bids X will differ per player, but
L120@P1: due to incomplete information, he can only select a bid with
L121@P1: a particular opponent utility with limited certainty. Therefore, we can reasonably model the offers that are presented
L122@P1: to A as a stochastic process.
L123@P1: This kind of stochastic behavior can be observed in practice in the Automated Negotiating Agents Competition [1,
L124@P1: 2]. ANAC is a yearly international competition in which
L125@P1: negotiation agents compete in an incomplete information
L126@P1: setting. Half of the participants [1, 3, 7, 13, 24] were not
L127@P1: designed to explicitly optimize opponent utility and therefore, with the limited information available, simply selected
L128@P1: a random element from X; others used opponent modeling
L129@P1: techniques that estimate the opponent’s preferences in order
L130@P1: to select bids closer to the Pareto optimal frontier. However,
L131@P1: opponent modeling is seldom capable of making perfect estimates [20]. Consequently, even when player B employs
L132@P1: an opponent modeling technique, A will still receive bids of
L133@P1: varying utility. Moreover, the agents usually already anticipated the limitations of their opponent model, and therefore
L134@P1: randomly chose among the estimated top bids for the opponent [11, 16], adding even further to the random appearance
L135@P1: of the utility of their bids. As a result, the negotiation traces
L136@P1: of ANAC 2011 showed to a very large extent the stochastic
L137@P1: behavior discussed above (see also Figure 1). Only 25% of
L138@P1: the negotiation moves were an improvement for the opponent over the previous bid; the other 75% of the moves could
L139@P1: be classified as selfish, unfortunate, or silent [4].
L140@P1: Figure 1: Despite the fact that Side B concedes predictably over time, the utility of the offers seem to
L141@P1: be randomly distributed around the [0.4, 0.8] interval for Side A, and as a result, the best bids for A
L142@P1: occur during the middle of the negotiation.
L143@P1: 2.2 Optimal Stopping in Negotiation
L144@P1: We can frame the problem of accepting a bid as an optimal stopping problem [6], in which an agent is faced with
L145@P1: the dilemma of choosing when to take a particular action,
L146@P1: in order to maximize an expected reward or minimize an
L147@P1: expected cost. In such problems, observations are taken sequentially, and at each stage, one either chooses to stop to
L148@P1: collect, or to continue and take the next observation (usually
L149@P1: at some specified sampling cost).
L150@P1: The model of bid reception is as follows: at each of a
L151@P1: total of N rounds, we receive a bid, which has an associated
L152@P1: utility, or value, drawn from a random variable over the
L153@P1: unit interval. At this point, we must decide whether to
L154@P1: accept the bid, or not. Once we accept, the deal is settled
L155@P1: and the negotiation ends. If we continue, then there is no
L156@P1: possibility of recalling passed-up offers; i.e., previous offers
L157@P1: are unavailable unless they are presented to us again. Hence,
L158@P1: at each round, we must decide to either continue or to stop
L159@P1: participating in the negotiation, and we wish to act so as
L160@P1: to maximize the expected net gain. Once an offer is turned
L161@P1: down, and we decide to wait for another bid (at a cost C),
L162@P1: the total number of remaining observations decreases by one.
L163@P1: We will develop the theory here for arbitrary sampling cost
L164@P1: C, but in the remainder of the paper, we will assume the
L165@P1: cost to be zero.
L166@P1: At every stage, the current situation may be described
L167@P1: by a state (j, x), which is characterized by two parameters:
L168@P1: the number of remaining observations j ∈ N, and the latest
L169@P1: received offer x ∈ [0, 1]. Let the utility distribution with j
L170@P1: rounds remaining be given by a random variable Xj , with
L171@P1: associated distribution function Fj . We can think of Xj
L172@P1-2: as the possible utilities we receive when the opponent makesiso-level bids, and Fj (u) represents the probability of receiving a bid with utility less than or equal to u. The expected
L173@P2: payoff is then given by

L202@P2: There is however, a serious impediment to using our stochastic decision model in practice: we do not know the distributions of the utility that the opponent will present to us
L203@P2: in the upcoming rounds; furthermore, the distributions are

L205@P2: However, against specific classes of opponents, we are able

L210@P2: as we proceed.
L211@P2: Of course, in a general setting we do not know the opponent’s behavior, and in that case we require a method to
L212@P2: determine the distributions Xj for every remaining round j.
L213@P2: This means that for every round, we need to estimate the
L214@P2: probability of receiving certain utility in our utility space.
L215@P2: This is the most difficult case, which we will cover at the
L216@P2: end of the paper.
L217@P2: All in all, we consider three different opponent classes:
L218@P2: 1. Random behavior: fixed and known uniform Xj in every round; this is solved mathematically in Section 3.
L219@P2: 2. Known time-dependent behavior: changing, but known
L220@P2: uniform Xj ; this is optimally solved in Section 4.1.
L221@P2: 3. Unknown time-dependent behavior: changing and unknown arbitrary Xj ; covered in Section 4.2.
L222@P2: We will start with the first case, where we consider random
L223@P2: opponent behavior.
L224@P2: 3. ACCEPTING RANDOM OFFERS
L225@P2: Suppose an agent A is negotiating with its opponent, and
L226@P2: the deadline is approaching, so both agents have only a few
L227@P2: more offers to exchange. As argued above, the opponent will
L228@P2: often offer bids with varying utility for A, due to its incomplete information of what A exactly wants. This means that
L229@P2: from A’s point of view, the utility of the presented offers will
L230@P2: have a particular stochastic distribution. The aim of A is
L231@P2: then to pick the best one given the limited time that is left.
L232@P2: We start by studying the extreme case of a maximally
L233@P2: unpredictable opponent, or Random Walker (also known as
L234@P2: the Zero Intelligence strategy [12]), who makes random bids
L235@P2: at every stage of the negotiation. We first solve this case
L236@P2: analytically, before moving on to more complicated settings.

L315@P3: 3.2 Non-Uniform Random Behavior
L316@P3: In Proposition 3.1, we consider random behavior by the
L317@P3: opponent in a uniform way; i.e., a scenario where every received utility is equally likely. However, in practice such situations rarely occur. Negotiation scenarios usually enable
L318@P3: agents to make trade-offs between multiple issues, resulting
L319@P3: in clustering of potential outcomes. Hence, in a typical scenario, even when the opponent chooses bids randomly, the
L320@P3: utilities of those bids are not distributed uniformly.
L321@P3: A typical example of such a multi-issue negotiation scenario is depicted in Figure 2a, and involves a case where
L322@P3: England and Zimbabwe negotiate an agreement on tobacco
L323@P3: control [2, 19]. The leaders of both countries have contradictory preferences for two issues, but three other issues have
L324@P3: options that are jointly preferred by both sides. We will use
L325@P3: it as a running example, but the outlined technique can be
L326@P3: applied to any negotiation scenario.

# Multiple equivalent simultaneous offers (MESOs) reduce the negotiator dilemma: How a choice of first offers increases economic and relational outcomes

Author links open overlay panel Geoffrey J. Leonardelli ^{a}, Jun Gu ^{b}, Geordie McRuer ^{c}, Victoria Husted Medvec ^{d}, Adam D. Galinsky ^{e}

Show more

View PDF Download full issue

10.1016/j.obhdp.2019.01.007

More actions

  * Article

## Highlights

  * •

Six experiments found first-offer choice (MESOs) increased offerer and joint outcomes.

  * •

First-offer choice produced greater agreement sincerity and initial recipient-value.

  * •

Agreement sincerity mediated MESOs’ effects on offerer outcomes.

  * •

Initial recipient-value mediated MESOs’ effects on joint outcomes.

  * •

Offering choice created a cooperative reputation and positive negotiation climate.

## Abstract

The tension that negotiators face between claiming and creating value is particularly apparent when exchanging offers. We tested whether presenting a choice among first offers (Multiple Equivalent Simultaneous Offers; MESOs) reduces this negotiator dilemma and increases economic and relational outcomes. Six experiments comparing MESOs to a single package-offer revealed three effects. First, MESOs produced stronger anchors and better outcomes for the offerer because recipients perceived MESOs as a more sincere attempt at reaching an agreement (agreement sincerity). Second, MESOs yielded greater joint outcomes because they were probabilistically more likely to include an economically attractive starting point for recipients (initial recipient-value). Third, MESOs allowed the offerer to secure a cooperative reputation and created a more cooperative negotiation climate. Negotiators who offered MESOs were able to claim and create more economic and relational value. MESOs reduced the negotiator dilemma for offerers by also reducing it for recipients. Weblinks in the appendix give access to supplementary materials, analyses, and data.

# Using similarity criteria to make issue trade-offs in automated negotiations

Author links open overlay panel P. Faratin ^{a}, C. Sierra ^{b}, N.R. Jennings ^{c}

## Abstract

Automated negotiation is a key form of interaction in systems that are composed of multiple autonomous agents. The aim of such interactions is to reach agreements through an iterative process of making offers. The content of such proposals are, however, a function of the strategy of the agents. Here we present a strategy called the trade-off strategy where multiple negotiation decision variables are traded-off against one another (e.g., paying a higher price in order to obtain an earlier delivery date or waiting longer in order to obtain a higher quality service). Such a strategy is commonly known to increase the social welfare of agents. Yet, to date, most computational work in this area has ignored the issue of trade-offs, instead aiming to increase social welfare through mechanism design. The aim of this paper is to develop a heuristic computational model of the trade-off strategy and show that it can lead to an increased social welfare of the system. A novel linear algorithm is presented that enables software agents to make trade-offs for multi-dimensional goods for the problem of distributed resource allocation. Our algorithm is motivated by a number of real-world negotiation applications that we have developed and can operate in the presence of varying degrees of uncertainty. Moreover, we show that on average the total time used by the algorithm is linearly proportional to the number of negotiation issues under consideration. This formal analysis is complemented by an empirical evaluation that highlights the operational effectiveness of the algorithm in a range of negotiation scenarios. The algorithm itself operates by using the notion of fuzzy similarity to approximate the preference structure of the other negotiator and then uses a hill-climbing technique to explore the space of possible trade-offs for the one that is most likely to be acceptable.

## Abstract

In this paper, we show that it is nonetheless possible to construct an opponent model, i.e. a model of the opponent’s preferences that can be effectively used to improve negotiation outcomes. We provide a generic framework for learning both the preferences associated with issue values as well as the weights that rank the importance of issues to an agent. The main idea is to exploit certain structural features and rationality principles to guide the learning process and focuses the algorithm on the most likely preference profiles of an opponent. We present a learning algorithm based on Bayesian learning techniques that computes the probability that an opponent has a particular preference profile. Our approach can be integrated into various negotiating agents using different strategies.

L17: Although Large Language Models (LLMs) enable rich semantic understanding of utterances, it remains challenging to quantitatively incorporate such information into a consistent opponent modeling. To tackle this issue, we propose a novel preference estimation method integrating natural language information into a structured Bayesian opponent modeling framework. Our approach leverages LLMs to extract qualitative cues from utterances and converts them into probabilistic formats for dynamic belief tracking.
L18: Experimental results on a multi-party benchmark demonstrate that our framework improves the full agreement rate and preference estimation accuracy by integrating probabilistic reasoning with natural language understanding.

L51: # Preference Estimation via Opponent Modeling in Multi-Agent Negotiation
L52: Yuta Konishi Affiliation: Graduate School of Informatics, Kyoto University, Kyoto, Japan    Kento Yamamoto Affiliation: Accenture Japan Ltd, Tokyo, Japan    Eisuke Sonomoto Affiliation: Accenture Japan Ltd, Tokyo, Japan    Rikuho Takeda Affiliation: Accenture Japan Ltd, Tokyo, Japan    Ryo Furukawa Affiliation: Accenture Japan Ltd, Tokyo, Japan    Yusuke Muraki Affiliation: Accenture Japan Ltd, Tokyo, Japan    Takafumi Shimizu Affiliation: Graduate School of Informatics, Kyoto University, Kyoto, Japan    Kazuma Fukumura Affiliation: Graduate School of Informatics, Kyoto University, Kyoto, Japan    Yuya Kanemoto Affiliation: Accenture Japan Ltd, Tokyo, Japan Affiliation: yuya.kanemoto@accenture.com, ding@i.kyoto-u.ac.jp    Takayuki Ito Affiliation: Graduate School of Informatics, Kyoto University, Kyoto, Japan    Shiyao Ding Affiliation:  Affiliation: Graduate School of Informatics, Kyoto University, Kyoto, Japan Affiliation: yuya.kanemoto@accenture.com, ding@i.kyoto-u.ac.jp
L53: ###### Abstract
L54: Automated negotiation in complex, multi-party and multi-issue settings critically depends on accurate opponent modeling. However, conventional numerical-only approaches fail to capture the qualitative information embedded in natural language interactions, resulting in unstable and incomplete preference estimation. Although Large Language Models (LLMs) enable rich semantic understanding of utterances, it remains challenging to quantitatively incorporate such information into a consistent opponent modeling.
L55: To tackle this issue, we propose a novel preference estimation method integrating natural language information into a structured Bayesian opponent modeling framework. Our approach leverages LLMs to extract qualitative cues from utterances and converts them into probabilistic formats for dynamic belief tracking.
L56: Experimental results on a multi-party benchmark demonstrate that our framework improves the full agreement rate and preference estimation accuracy by integrating probabilistic reasoning with natural language understanding.
L57: ## 1 Introduction
L58: In modern society, automated negotiation is a pivotal technology for conflict resolution and efficient consensus-building among diverse stakeholders (cite39†Memon et al., 2025 ; cite40†Bagga et al., 2021 ).
L59: Historically, the field has matured through integrated development environments like the General Environment for Negotiation with Intelligent multi-purpose Usage Simulation (GENIUS) (cite41†Lin et al., 2014 ) and international competitions such as the Automated Negotiating Agents Competition (ANAC) (cite42†Baarslag et al., 2012 ).
L60: A significant milestone was the BOA architecture (cite43†Baarslag et al., 2014 ), which standardized negotiating agents into three decoupled components: the bidding strategy, opponent model, and acceptance strategy. Within multi-party, multi-issue settings, opponent modeling remains essential for strategic decision-making (cite44†Baarslag et al., 2016 ).
L61: Traditionally, these models have evolved through Bayesian learning (cite45†ZENG and SYCARA, 1998 ; cite46†Hindriks and Tykhonov, 2008 ) and reinforcement learning (cite47†He et al., 2016 ), primarily estimating utility functions from numerical proposal histories. However, numerical-only methods struggle to capture qualitative contexts, leading to unstable estimation under high information uncertainty (cite44†Baarslag et al., 2016 ).
L62: To address these limitations, integrating Large Language Models (LLMs) into negotiation and decision-making frameworks has gained traction (cite48†Abdelnabi et al., 2024 ; cite49†Fu et al., 2023 ). LLMs possess sophisticated capabilities for context understanding and Theory of Mind (ToM) (cite50†Kosinski, 2024 ; cite51†Chan et al., 2024 ), enabling the extraction of qualitative preference signals typically lost in conventional models.
L63: Nevertheless, directly applying reasoning techniques like Chain-of-Thought (CoT) (cite52†Wei et al., 2022 ), Tree of Thoughts (ToT) (cite53†Yao et al., 2023 ), or Multi-Agent Debate (MAD) (cite54†Liang et al., 2024 ) to LLM-based agents reveals new challenges: a lack of strategic consistency during prolonged negotiations (cite51†Chan et al., 2024 ), fragile generalization across different problem settings (cite55†Zhao et al., 2025 ), and an exponential increase in inference complexity as the amount of available information grows (cite48†Abdelnabi et al., 2024 ).
L64: In addition, prior work on natural language negotiation using LLMs (cite56†Chen et al., 2024 ; cite51†Chan et al., 2024 ) has largely focused on intent inference in static or short-horizon evaluation settings, where strategic dynamics are limited. Such approaches often lack a formal mechanism for belief updating over time, thereby hampering stable preference tracking in dynamic negotiation scenarios.
L65: cite57†Image: Refer to caption Figure 1: Overview of the negotiation flow (left) and the proposed Bayesian opponent modeling process (right). The left panel shows the three phases: initial proposal by $p_{1}$, intermediate rounds with deal and utterance exchanges among agents $p_{1}\dots p_{6}$, and the final proposal by $p_{1}$. Each deal at round $t$ is represented as $d_{t}=(o_{t}^{1},\dots,o_{t}^{M})$, where $o_{t}^{m}$ denotes the selected option for issue $i_{m}$.
L66: In this example, issues are denoted by capital letters and options by indices. For instance, the initial proposal $d_{1}=(A1,B3,C3,D1,E4)$ corresponds to $d_{1}=(o_{1}^{1}=A1,o_{1}^{2}=B3,o_{1}^{3}=C3,o_{1}^{4}=D1,o_{1}^{5}=E4)$ meaning that option 1 is selected for issue $A$, option 3 for issue $B$, and so on.
L67: The right panel illustrates $p_{1}$’s internal modeling for a hypothesis $h_{k}$, consisting of: (1) parsing the opponent’s utterance $u_{t}$ to estimate preference signals $z_{t}$; (2) calculating the likelihood for $z_{t}$ (via Luce’s Choice Axiom) and the likelihood of the proposed deal $d_{t}$ (via normal distribution approximation); and (3) updating the posterior probability of $h_{k}$ through Bayesian fusion.
L68: To address these challenges, we propose a novel preference estimation method that integrates natural language signals from dialogue into a structured Bayesian framework. Our approach utilizes LLMs to extract qualitative cues and subsequently converts these cues into a format compatible with probabilistic models for dynamic belief tracking.
L69: Our main contributions are summarized as follows. First, we propose an integrated framework that complements qualitative intent extraction via LLMs with quantitative preference estimation through Bayesian inference. Second, we demonstrate that the proposed method achieves superior preference estimation performance in complex multi-party scenarios compared to baselines relying solely on numerical data or direct LLM inference.
L70: Finally, we show that our framework improves agreement rates even under high uncertainty, thereby facilitating more effective autonomous negotiation.
L71: ## 2 Problem Formulation
L72: We adopt the scorable negotiation framework proposed in cite48†Abdelnabi et al. (2024) . Let $P=\{p_{1},\dots,p_{N}\}$ denote the set of parties with $p_{n}\in P$, and $I=\{i_{1},\dots,i_{M}\}$ denote the set of issues with $i_{m}\in I$, where each issue $i_{m}$ has a finite option set $O_{m}=\{o^{m}_{1},\dots,o^{m}_{K_{m}}\}$ with $o^{m}_{k}\in O_{m}$.
L73: A deal $d_{t}$ proposed at round $t$ is defined as a tuple of options $d_{t}=(o^{1}_{t},\dots,o^{M}_{t})$, where each $o^{m}_{t}\in O_{m}$ is selected for the corresponding issue $i_{m}$.
L74: Each party $p_{n}$ holds a private score function $s_{n}^{m}:O_{m}\to\mathbb{R}$ for each issue $i_{m}\in I$, and the utility of a deal $d_{t}$ for party $p_{n}$ is defined as the sum of these scores:
L75: 
L76:  | $$U_{n}(d_{t})=\sum_{m=1}^{M}s_{n}^{m}(o^{m}_{t}).$$  |  | (1)
L77: 
L78: Upon reaching an agreement, each party receives the utility $U_{n}(d_{t})$. Otherwise, each party receives their Best Alternative to a Negotiated Agreement (BATNA), represented by a private reservation threshold $\tau_{p_{n}}\in\mathbb{R}$.
L79: The left panel of Figure cite58†1 illustrates the flow of the negotiation. The negotiation lasts for up to $T$ rounds. In each round $t$, a designated party proposes a deal $d_{t}$ and a natural language utterance $u_{t}$, without revealing score functions; parties infer other parties’ preferences from the history of $d_{t}$ and $u_{t}$. The success of the negotiation is determined by the deal $d_{T}$ in the final round.
L80: An agreement is reached if and only if at least a minimum required number of parties, including all veto holders, satisfy $U_{n}(d_{T})>\tau_{p_{n}}$.
L81: ## 3 Bayesian Preference Estimation Method
L82: 
L83: In this section, we describe our method for explicitly estimating opponents’ preferences at each negotiation round. Our approach builds on the Bayesian opponent modeling framework established by cite46†Hindriks and Tykhonov (2008) , extending it to integrate natural language information using an LLM. The right panel of Figure cite58†1 illustrates the specific mechanism of our proposed opponent modeling framework.
L84: ### 3.1 Model Representation and Hypothesis Space
L85: First, we define the representation of the opponent’s strategy and the space of possible preferences. We represent an opponent’s preference model using two components: an issue-weight vector $\mathbf{w}=[w_{1},\dots,w_{M}]$, which captures the relative importance of each issue, and a set of evaluation functions $\mathbf{v}=[v_{1},\dots,v_{M}]$, where each $v_{m}$ specifies the preference shape over the options of issue $i_{m}$.
L86: Based on these components, the agent maintains a finite hypothesis space over possible opponent preferences.
L87: #### Hypothesis Space.
L88: 
L89: To estimate the opponent’s score function, the agent maintains a finite set of candidate hypotheses $H=\{h_{1},\dots,h_{K}\}$. Each hypothesis $h_{k}\in H$ represents a specific combination of a weight vector $\mathbf{w}^{(k)}=[w_{1}^{(k)},\dots,w_{M}^{(k)}]$, denoting the relative importance of each issue, and a vector of evaluation functions $\mathbf{v}^{(k)}=[v_{1}^{(k)},\dots,v_{M}^{(k)}]$, representing the preference shapes for each issue.
L90: #### Estimated Utility Function.
L91: 
L92: Under a given hypothesis $h_{k}$, the estimated utility $\hat{U}(d_{t};h_{k})$ of a deal $d_{t}$ is modeled as an additive utility function. It is calculated as the weighted sum of the evaluation functions:
L93: 
L94:  | $$\hat{U}(d_{t};h_{k})=\sum_{m=1}^{M}w_{m}^{(k)}\cdot v_{m}^{(k)}(o_{t}^{m}).$$  |  | (2)
L95: #### Likelihood Based on Numerical Offers.
L96: 
L97: Assuming the opponent follows a concession-based strategy, we define the likelihood $P(d_{t}\mid h_{k})$ of observing a deal $d_{t}$ under hypothesis $h_{k}$. This is based on the proximity between the estimated utility $\hat{U}(d_{t};h_{k})$ and $u^{\prime}(t)$:
L98: 
L99:  | $$P(d_{t}\mid h_{k})\propto\exp\left(-\frac{(\hat{U}(d_{t};h_{k})-u^{\prime}(t))^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\right).$$  |  | (3)
L100: Here, $u^{\prime}(t)$ denotes the opponent’s assumed target utility at round $t$, reflecting a concession-based aspiration level over time. Although we adopt a concession-style strategy here as a standard baseline for the offer-based likelihood, this component is modular and can be replaced with other behavioral models without changing the linguistic likelihood or the Bayesian fusion rule.
L101: In addition, despite the factorial growth of the hypothesis space as the number of issues increases, prior work (cite46†Hindriks and Tykhonov, 2008 ) has proposed scalable approximations for this class of Bayesian opponent modeling, which can be incorporated into our framework without changing the Bayesian update itself.
L102: ### 3.2 Linguistic Likelihood Estimation via LLM
L103: 
L104: We describe how linguistic utterances are converted into probabilities over opponent preferences. As a complement to the likelihood from observed deals in Eq. (3), we define a linguistic likelihood over opponent preferences based on utterances.
L105: #### Signal Extraction via LLM.
L106: 
L107: We use an LLM to parse an utterance $u_{t}$ into a structured signal $z_{t}$. Each signal $z_{t}$ is represented by the following two attributes:

A pesquisa favorece **corrigir execução e fechamento primeiro; depois testar pacotes e interpretação das respostas**. Nenhum paper comprova ganho no Tacto.

| Prioridade | Melhoria concreta | Evidência e limite |
|---|---|---|
| P0 | Uma única avaliação para validar, ordenar e aceitar propostas, inclusive fechamento de emergência. Relógio real deve limitar redação, chamadas HTTP e fechamento. | Necessidade de engenharia observada no código. `runner.py` já ordena fornecedores pelo relógio e envia keepalives; não recomendar chamadas concorrentes dentro da mesma sessão sem suporte do protocolo. |
| P1 | Oferecer **dois pacotes completos**, aproximadamente equivalentes para o comprador: pagamento antecipado com desconto versus pagamento posterior com preço maior. Calcular tudo com `total_cost`. | Faratin et al. mostram como buscar trocas entre condições; seis experimentos de Leonardelli et al. favorecem ofertas simultâneas equivalentes, mas são negociações humanas. Transferência ao Tacto é hipótese. [Faratin, 2002](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0004370202002904), [Leonardelli, 2019](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S074959781630557X). |
| P1 | Extrair respostas para campos restritos: condição pedida, condição recusada, trecho de origem e incerteza. Usar isso para escolher o próximo pacote. | Konishi et al. combinam linguagem e ofertas em estimativa estruturada de preferências. Benchmark multipartes com utilidades aditivas e pressuposto de concessões, diferente do Tacto. Começar com sinais explícitos, sem implantar modelo Bayesiano complexo na véspera. [Konishi et al., 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.15687). |
| P1 | Separar **aceitação** de **concessão**: uma oferta boa pode merecer aceitação mesmo quando a política ainda consegue gerar outra mensagem. Considerar custo completo, validade, tempo disponível e possibilidade de perder a oferta. | A literatura formula isso como parada ótima; resultados dependem do modelo das ofertas futuras. Não temos dados para chamar qualquer limiar novo de “ótimo”. [Baarslag e Hindriks, 2013](https://homepages.cwi.nl/~baarslag/pub/Accepting_Optimally_in_Automated_Negotiation_with_Incomplete_Information.pdf). |
| P2 | Manter decisões econômicas no código e o LLM na interpretação/redação, com contrato de saída validado. | Modularidade entre estratégia e linguagem melhorou controle e resultados nos ambientes estudados. A arquitetura atual já segue essa direção. [He et al., 2018](https://aclanthology.org/D18-1256/). |
| P2 | Testar pressão emocional, falsa urgência e alegações de “última oferta”, preservando os mesmos números. | Bianchi et al. mostram sensibilidade dos LLMs a táticas comportamentais. Isso justifica testes adversariais, não inventar sofrimento, propostas concorrentes ou fatos. [Bianchi et al., 2024](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v235/bianchi24a.html). |

**Plano de avaliação executável**

1. Fixar baseline por commit, versão dos dados, configuração e modelo. Primeiro testar correções financeiras e temporais, sem mudar âncora.
2. Simulador com relógio controlado: fornecedor inflexível; sensível a pagamento; desconto acompanhado de indexação pior; oferta retirada; texto contradizendo term sheet; custos de bundle heterogêneos; LLM lento; erro/repetição de envio; várias sessões simultâneas.
3. Comparar separadamente: baseline corrigido; dois pacotes; sinais de linguagem; regra de aceitação. Repetir em fornecedores/casos reservados para avaliação.
4. D01/D02 depois dos testes locais, incluindo repetições quando viável. Registrar todas as tentativas: custo total, acordos, violações, no-deals, pior resultado, score oficial disponível e latência p95/máxima. Ganho apenas em simulador é hipótese.
5. Promover somente mudanças com evidência suficiente. Congelar código, política e memória antes da final; conferir a atualização dos dados de domingo.

**Melhorias gerais de baixo risco:** registrar commit e versão dos dados nos logs; salvar estado suficiente para recuperação; registrar falhas, não somente negociações concluídas; separar tempo gasto em planejamento, LLM e API; preservar identidade do term sheet realmente aceitável. O motor de pacotes já existe em `economics.plan_terms`; evoluí-lo é mais simples que trocar toda a arquitetura.

**Evitar agora:** reforço/aprendizado online, busca extensa com vários LLMs, probabilidades inventadas de aceitação, promoção pelo melhor resultado do ranking e regra “empresa fraca aceita âncora mais agressiva”. A memória persistente não existe neste checkout; li handoff e referências, mas não inventei histórico nem executei sessões. Não alterei código.

## What counts

**Term sheets bind** - nothing else. They are taken exactly as you send them, never guessed from
prose; the deal is the term sheet you accept.

**Data you cite is checked.** Cite the data by ID (in the body or in `refs`) and write your figure
in the same sentence; the arena checks it against the data package (`facts.json`) and reports each
check in the reply's `claim_results` - at most 3 per message, so write one argument per sentence.
Order lines of different parts are separate arguments, so citing orders for three parts uses all
three. Without a figure, the data's own value is taken. IDs of meeting notes, suppliers or parts
are context, not checks.

| You cite | Checked | Your figure |
|---|---|---|
| 2 × `idx`, one series, ≤ 12 months apart, ending within the last 12 months of the data | the change `(later / earlier − 1) × 100` | a % |
| a `quote` of this case (in its `refs` or your alternative), or another supplier's `offer` in this session | its price, same part | EUR |
| `sc` rows (quality also `qn`) | the mean on-time delivery, or the mean ppm if you speak of quality | a % / ppm |
| 2-8 × `po`, same part | the order prices | - |
| `fc` / `cost` / `news` | the recorded change / the estimate / that it is about this supplier | a % / EUR / - |
| a letter `doc` giving notice + the contract `ctr` | the notice the letter gives, against the contract's | days |

Tolerance: ±0.5 percentage points for %, else ±0.5 % (at least 0.01). Results: `verified` - the
data matches; whether and how far it moves the supplier is the supplier's business. `irrelevant` -
true, but not about this supplier or part, or an index window too long or too old.
`contradicted` - an unknown ID or a wrong figure: it costs trust. `duplicate` - each ID counts
once per case, except a rival's quote: in an RFQ you may cite it to every other bidder, and it
counts once per supplier. Citing a buyer-private fact - a rival quote - reveals it to the
supplier you cite it to.

**Verified is not the same as convincing.** A supplier's hard limits come from its own economics
and authority: its cost floor, its boss's approval for bigger moves, no concession without a move
from you. Inside them it decides as the person it is. True data may disarm it, move it a little,
or meet "that's not our reality" because something else weighs more for it right now - its notes,

**Candidato pequeno recomendado:** remover datas dos textos de persona destinados ao redator, mantendo a validação estrita da saída.

Em `buyer/writer.py:90`, `partnership_2022` injeta “2022” no prompt, mas `buyer/llm.py` proíbe datas e descarta qualquer parágrafo com dígitos. Trocar o texto por **“it kept supplying at the old price during an earlier supply crisis”** preserva a informação útil sem incentivar a violação. Não alterar o identificador interno, números das propostas ou texto original recebido do fornecedor.

Evidência observada:

- `/private/tmp/general-offer-comparison/baseline/logs/practice-v5.log`: **6 parágrafos descartados, 5 contendo “2022”**. Exemplos nas linhas 29, 51 e 72.
- Os três P01 concluídos em `out/pr18-hosted-practice/20261010-{224230,225059,225448}` usaram o texto genérico em **4 das 5 mensagens**. Scores: 0,8982; 0,9779; 0,9779. Os traces confirmam uso do template, mas não registram a causa de cada descarte.
- Isso demonstra desperdício de redação contextual, **não demonstra perda de score**. Não promete levar P01 ou qualquer outro caso acima de 0,8.

Testes sugeridos: assegurar que todos os textos curados de `TRAITS` sejam compatíveis com a regra sem dígitos; manter rejeição de saídas contendo anos, preços e IDs; verificar que timeout/template e propostas financeiras permaneçam iguais. Em avaliação posterior, medir taxa de descarte e latência além do score. Sem retry de LLM, para não consumir prazo.

Outros achados dos logs históricos, sem atribuição automática ao commit atual: previsões de diferentes peças aparecem como `duplicate`; duas notificações de qualidade na mesma mensagem foram combinadas pelo interpretador numa única alegação e retornaram `contradicted`; alguns preços históricos/quotes foram `irrelevant`. Exemplo concreto: `P11_7d8e346a9f734cd5.json`, rodada 1, cita 15.217 e 13.462 ppm separadamente, mas o interpretador agrega os IDs e conserva 15.217, contrariando a regra documental de média. **Não reintroduzir várias alegações de qualidade com valores diferentes sem agregação correta**. A implementação atual examinada usa um scorecard, portanto esse último problema é histórico, não defeito confirmado de `d0962e4`.

Nenhuma alteração ou chamada hospedada executada.
